items.prompt: What does XSS stand for?
choices: Cross-site scripting
Extended session scripting
Cross-server syncing
External script scanning
items.explanation: XSS is the standard abbreviation for cross-site scripting.

items.prompt: In XSS, whose browser actually runs the attacker's script?
choices: The victim's own browser
Only the attacker's browser
The web server's browser-based admin panel
No browser — it runs purely server-side
items.explanation: XSS specifically means the script executes inside the victim's own browser, not the attacker's or the server's.

items.prompt: In an XSS attack, under whose session does the injected script run?
choices: The victim's own logged-in session
A brand-new anonymous session created just for the script
The attacker's own separate session
No session is involved at all
items.explanation: That's the defining danger of XSS — the script runs with the victim's own session already attached.

items.prompt: What's the core mistake that makes XSS possible?
choices: A page treats user-supplied input as trusted code instead of as plain data
A server uses an outdated version of HTTP
A user picks a weak password
A database table is missing an index
items.explanation: XSS happens when user input gets interpreted as executable code rather than displayed as text.

items.prompt: Which of these is the clearest example of an XSS payload?
choices: A comment containing `<script>stealCookies()</script>`
A comment containing the plain text 'great post!'
A request with a missing Content-Type header
A password that's too short
items.explanation: A `<script>` tag smuggled into content that gets rendered as HTML is the textbook XSS payload.

items.prompt: True or false: XSS requires the attacker to already know the victim's password.
choices: False
True
True, but only for stored XSS
True, but only for reflected XSS
items.explanation: XSS never requires knowing the victim's credentials — it rides along on the victim's own already-authenticated browser session.

items.prompt: Why is 'cross-site' part of the name, even though the Scenario's attack happens entirely on one site?
choices: Because the injected script can act as if it came from the vulnerable site, while effectively acting on the attacker's behalf, blurring the line between the site's own code and attacker code
Because the attack literally requires two different websites to be open in two different browser tabs at once
Because XSS only works across subdomains, never on a single domain
The name is historical and has no real meaning today
items.explanation: The 'cross-site' framing refers to attacker-controlled behavior effectively acting across the trust boundary between site and attacker, not to needing two open tabs.

items.prompt: If a site had zero logged-in users, would stored XSS in its comments still be a security problem?
choices: Yes — it could still deface the page, redirect visitors, or run other scripts against anonymous visitors
No — XSS is only ever dangerous if a session cookie exists to steal
No — without login, a browser simply refuses to run any script
Yes, but only because anonymous visitors always have passwords anyway
items.explanation: Stealing a session cookie is one consequence of XSS, not the only one — an injected script can do anything regular page script could do to any visitor, logged in or not.

items.prompt: A site escapes nothing, but requires users to log in before posting a comment. Does requiring login prevent the Scenario's stored XSS attack?
choices: No — the attacker still just needs an account to post the comment; every other visitor who views it is still at risk, logged in or not
Yes — login requirements fully prevent XSS by definition
Yes, but only because logged-in users can't post script tags
No, but only because login forms are themselves vulnerable to XSS
items.explanation: Requiring login only controls who can post — it does nothing about how posted content gets rendered. The vulnerability is in the renderer, not the authentication gate.
items.reflection: The underlying idea — a system trusting 'this came through our own normal input channel' as proof it's safe — shows up well beyond the web: a CLI tool that executes a config file's contents as shell commands, or a mail server that runs macros embedded in an attachment. Where else have you seen 'it came from inside our own system' mistaken for 'it's safe to execute'?

items.prompt: A teammate says: 'XSS and CSRF are basically the same thing — both abuse a victim's logged-in session, so one fix covers both.' What's wrong with that claim?
choices: They share a victim (a logged-in session) but not a mechanism: XSS injects and runs attacker code in the browser, while CSRF forges a request without injecting any code at all — each needs its own, different defense
Nothing is wrong — treating them as the same problem is correct and saves effort
The claim is wrong only because CSRF is strictly more dangerous than XSS
The claim is wrong only because XSS requires HTTPS and CSRF doesn't
items.explanation: Sharing a victim isn't the same as sharing a mechanism — conflating the two leads to 'fixing' XSS with a CSRF token (which does nothing about injected script) or vice versa.

items.prompt: A chat app renders usernames as-is inside a `` on every message. An attacker registers the username ``. Is this an XSS risk even though the attacker never touched the message body at all?
choices: Yes — any user-controlled field rendered unescaped into HTML is a potential XSS vector, not just a 'message' or 'comment' field specifically
No — XSS can only happen through a field explicitly called a comment or message
No — usernames are always sanitized automatically by every framework
Yes, but only if the username field also requires an email verification step
items.explanation: XSS isn't tied to any particular field name — it's about any user-controlled value being rendered as HTML markup instead of text. A username field is just as dangerous as a comment field if it's inserted unescaped.

items.prompt: What does CSRF stand for?
choices: Cross-site request forgery
Cross-server resource fetch
Client-side rendering failure
Credential storage rotation failure
items.explanation: CSRF is the standard abbreviation for cross-site request forgery.

items.prompt: In a CSRF attack, who actually sends the forged request?
choices: The victim's own browser, automatically attaching the victim's existing credentials
The attacker's own browser, using stolen credentials
The vulnerable site's own server, by itself
No request is actually sent — it's purely theoretical
items.explanation: CSRF specifically relies on the victim's browser sending the request with credentials the browser attaches automatically.

items.prompt: Does CSRF require injecting any code onto the vulnerable site?
choices: No — it exploits the browser's automatic credential-attaching behavior from an entirely different page
Yes — CSRF always requires a script tag on the vulnerable site, same as XSS
Yes, but only a CSS-based injection
No, but only because CSRF only works without any credentials at all
items.explanation: CSRF needs no code on the vulnerable site at all — the forged request originates from somewhere else entirely (another page, an email link).

items.prompt: What does a victim need to have, for a CSRF attack against a given site to work?
choices: An active, already-logged-in session on that site
A weak password on that site
The site's source code
A browser extension installed
items.explanation: CSRF rides on an existing authenticated session — without one, there's nothing for the forged request to exploit.

items.prompt: Which of these is a classic CSRF scenario?
choices: A hidden auto-submitting form on an attacker's page that quietly posts a money transfer to a bank you're logged into
A comment field that renders a `<script>` tag as real markup
A password field that accepts any string without validation
A server that logs every request it receives
items.explanation: The hidden-form-on-another-site pattern, relying on automatically-attached credentials, is the textbook CSRF shape.

items.prompt: What's the typical fix for CSRF?
choices: Verifying the request actually came from the site's own page, e.g. via a CSRF token
Escaping HTML special characters before rendering output
Using a stronger password hashing algorithm
Adding more server memory
items.explanation: CSRF tokens (or equivalent same-site defenses) prove the request originated from the site's own UI — a completely different mechanism from output escaping.

items.prompt: True or false: a CSRF attack can succeed entirely through a link in an email, with no script required on the vulnerable site.
choices: True
False
True, but only if the email itself contains a script tag
False, because email clients always block all external links
items.explanation: A crafted link or auto-submitting form delivered via email, another site, or an ad can trigger a CSRF request — no code injection on the vulnerable site is needed.

items.prompt: Would sanitizing a bank's comment field help prevent the bank-transfer CSRF example?
choices: No — CSRF doesn't involve the bank's comment field at all; it exploits a request forged from somewhere else entirely
Yes — sanitization and CSRF protection are the same mechanism
Yes, but only if the comment field accepts HTML
No, but only because banks don't have comment fields
items.explanation: CSRF and a comment field's sanitization are unrelated — the forged request doesn't pass through any of the bank's own input fields.

items.prompt: A site adds HTML escaping everywhere user content is rendered, closing every XSS hole. Is it now also protected against CSRF?
choices: No — escaping prevents injected code from executing, but CSRF doesn't involve injecting code at all; it needs a separate defense like a CSRF token
Yes — escaping output is a complete fix for both XSS and CSRF
Yes, but only on pages that also use cookies
No, but only because escaping slows down the server too much to matter
items.explanation: Escaping output closes the XSS hole specifically — it has no effect on CSRF, which is a forged-request problem, not a rendering problem.
items.reflection: CSRF's core trick — a system automatically trusting a credential that travels with every request, regardless of where the request actually originated — shows up outside the browser too: an API key baked into a mobile app that any copy of the app can replay, or a signed cookie that a proxy forwards without checking where the original request came from. Where else have you seen 'this request carries valid credentials' mistaken for 'this request is legitimate'?

items.prompt: A password-reset endpoint is a simple `GET /reset-password?email=victim@example.com` with no confirmation step and no CSRF token. An attacker embeds that exact URL as an `` tag on a forum post. What happens when a logged-in admin's browser loads that forum page?
choices: The admin's browser automatically requests the image URL, silently triggering the password reset as a side effect — a CSRF-style forced action, delivered via something as simple as an image tag
Nothing happens, because image tags can never trigger GET requests to arbitrary URLs
The attack fails automatically because GET requests never carry cookies
The attack fails because password resets always require typing a password first
items.explanation: Browsers fetch whatever URL an `` points to, cookies and all — if a sensitive action lives behind a plain GET with no extra proof of intent, an image tag is enough to trigger it on any victim who merely views the page.

items.prompt: A site generates a CSRF token but checks it loosely: it just checks that *some* token was submitted, not that it matches the one issued to that specific session. Is this a meaningful CSRF defense?
choices: No — an attacker can harvest any valid-looking token (even their own) and submit it alongside the forged request, since the check never verifies it belongs to the victim's session
Yes — the mere presence of a token field is sufficient, regardless of its value
Yes, because tokens are always unique per request by default
No, but only because tokens must be encrypted, not just present
items.explanation: A CSRF token only works if the server verifies it matches the one tied to that specific session — checking for mere presence lets an attacker supply any token at all, defeating the point.

items.prompt: What's the general goal of 'sanitization' in this unit's context?
choices: User input must stay data, never become code
User input must be deleted before storage
User input must always be encrypted at rest
User input must be limited to 140 characters
items.explanation: Sanitization's broad goal is keeping user-supplied content inert as data, never letting it be interpreted as executable code.

items.prompt: What's the specific technique this unit uses to implement sanitization?
choices: Escaping/output encoding — converting HTML-control characters into safe text
Deleting any comment containing the word 'script'
Requiring comments to be under 50 characters
Encrypting comments before storing them
items.explanation: The unit's concrete technique is escaping/output encoding: converting structural HTML characters into their literal text equivalents.

items.prompt: If a comment's text is properly escaped before being rendered, is the visitor able to read what the original commenter actually typed?
choices: Yes — escaping preserves the content exactly, it just prevents it from being parsed as markup
No — escaped text is always replaced with a generic placeholder
No — escaping deletes any character it can't recognize
Yes, but only the first few words
items.explanation: Escaping doesn't remove or hide content — it keeps the exact text while ensuring the browser treats it as literal text, not as markup.

items.prompt: Which characters are typically escaped to prevent user text from being parsed as HTML markup?
choices: Structural characters like <, >, ", ', and &
Only lowercase letters
Only numeric digits
Only whitespace characters
items.explanation: The characters that give HTML its structural meaning (<, >, ", ', &) are exactly the ones escaping needs to neutralize.

items.prompt: Is 'sanitization' the same thing as 'deleting all user-submitted content'?
choices: No — sanitization's goal is to keep content but render it as inert data, not to delete it
Yes — those two terms are interchangeable in this unit
Yes, but only for comments longer than one sentence
No, but only because deletion is technically impossible
items.explanation: Sanitization preserves what the user wrote; it just ensures it's never executed as code — it isn't a deletion mechanism.

items.prompt: Would blocking any comment that contains the literal word 'script' count as proper sanitization?
choices: No — that's a weak blocklist, easily bypassed by other tags or attack syntax that don't contain that word
Yes — blocking that one keyword closes the XSS risk completely
Yes, as long as the check is case-insensitive
No, but only because the word 'script' is too short to detect reliably
items.explanation: A keyword blocklist is a much weaker defense than escaping — it's trivially bypassed by syntax that doesn't happen to contain the blocked word.

items.prompt: Sanitization is described as preventing what, specifically?
choices: The injection of attacker-controlled code in the first place
Slow page load times
Users from submitting very long comments
Server disk space from filling up
items.explanation: Sanitization is squarely about preventing code injection — it's not a performance or storage mechanism.

items.prompt: True or false: sanitization only matters for content that gets permanently stored, like a saved comment.
choices: False — any user input rendered into a page needs sanitizing, whether stored or just reflected back
True — only stored content is ever dangerous
True, but only for comments specifically, not other fields
False, but only for content submitted via GET requests
items.explanation: Reflected XSS (covered later) shows that even non-stored, echoed-back input is just as dangerous if it's rendered unescaped.

items.prompt: A developer sanitizes comments by stripping out the literal substring `<script>` (case-insensitively) before rendering. Does this fully sanitize the content?
choices: No — this is a blocklist approach that misses other injection vectors entirely, like `` or a script tag split with extra attributes
Yes — stripping that one substring removes every possible XSS vector
Yes, as long as it also strips the word `javascript`
No, but only because the substring check should run after rendering instead of before
items.explanation: Blocklisting specific substrings never closes the general mechanism — any syntax that achieves script execution without using the literal blocked string sails right through.
items.reflection: The core idea — data must stay data and never be reinterpreted as instructions by whatever reads it next — recurs well beyond HTML: SQL injection (user input landing inside a query string instead of a parameter), log injection (user input landing inside a log line parsed by automated tooling), or a template engine executing a filename passed in as a 'theme' setting. Where else have you seen user-supplied data get treated as instructions instead of as inert content?

items.prompt: A site escapes `<` and `>` in user comments, but not `"` or `'`. The comment is later inserted into an HTML attribute like `<div title="USER_TEXT">`. Is this escaping sufficient for that context?
choices: No — leaving quote characters unescaped still lets an attacker break out of the attribute value and inject new attributes or event handlers
Yes — escaping < and > alone is always sufficient in any HTML context
Yes, because attribute values can't contain injected code regardless of quoting
No, but only because title attributes are never actually rendered by browsers
items.explanation: Which characters matter structurally depends on where the text lands — inside an attribute value, the quote character that delimits it is just as dangerous as < and > are inside element text.

items.prompt: A site sanitizes every comment field but forgets to sanitize the 'display name' field shown next to each comment. Is the site still vulnerable to XSS overall?
choices: Yes — sanitization has to cover every place user-controlled content gets rendered, not just the field that seems like the 'obvious' risk
No — as long as the main comment text is sanitized, the whole page is safe
No, because display names are always limited to plain alphabetic characters by the browser
Yes, but only if the display name field also accepts emoji
items.explanation: A single unsanitized field anywhere user content reaches the page is enough for a full XSS vulnerability — sanitization has to be applied comprehensively, not selectively.

items.prompt: What does CSP stand for?
choices: Content Security Policy
Cross-Site Protection
Cookie Session Protocol
Client Security Protocol
items.explanation: CSP stands for Content Security Policy.

items.prompt: What kind of thing is a CSP, mechanically?
choices: An HTTP header that tells the browser which sources of scripts and other resources are allowed to load and execute
A database table listing banned users
A JavaScript library that runs inside the page
A type of session cookie
items.explanation: CSP is delivered as an HTTP response header, enforced by the browser itself.

items.prompt: What is CSP's relationship to sanitization, per L1?
choices: A second, independent layer that limits damage if an injection somehow still gets through
A full replacement for sanitization that makes it unnecessary
An alternative name for the exact same technique as sanitization
A technique used only to defend against CSRF, not XSS
items.explanation: L1 frames CSP as a complementary second layer, not a substitute for sanitization.

items.prompt: Who enforces a site's CSP rules?
choices: The visitor's own browser
The site's database
A third-party certificate authority
The visitor's internet service provider
items.explanation: CSP is enforced client-side, by the browser itself, based on the header the server sent.

items.prompt: Does having a CSP mean a site no longer needs to sanitize its output?
choices: No — CSP is a safety net for when the primary defense fails, not a replacement for it
Yes — a correctly configured CSP removes the need for sanitization entirely
Yes, but only for sites with no login system
No, but only because browsers ignore CSP headers by default
items.explanation: CSP is explicitly a backstop, not a substitute for sanitizing input in the first place.

items.prompt: What does CSP restrict, in general terms?
choices: What sources of scripts, styles, and other resources are allowed to load and execute on a page
How many requests per second a server can handle
How long a user session is allowed to stay active
Which countries can access the site
items.explanation: CSP is about restricting allowed resource sources and script execution, not rate limiting, sessions, or geography.

items.prompt: If a sanitization bug somewhere lets a malicious script slip into the page's HTML, can a correctly configured CSP still help?
choices: Yes — it can block that script from executing or from sending data out, even though it made it into the markup
No — once a script is in the HTML, nothing can stop it from running
Yes, but only if the script is less than 100 characters long
No, because CSP only applies to scripts loaded from external files
items.explanation: This is exactly CSP's purpose as a second layer — stopping execution or exfiltration even after an injection has already landed in the markup.

items.prompt: True or false: CSP needs to know about a site's specific comment-rendering logic to work.
choices: False — it's a blanket, browser-enforced rule that doesn't need to know anything about where content comes from
True — a separate CSP rule has to be written for every input field
True, but only for comment fields specifically
False, but only because CSP is deprecated and no longer enforced
items.explanation: CSP operates as a general rule about what's allowed to run or load — it doesn't need any awareness of specific application logic.

items.prompt: A site has a strict CSP that blocks inline scripts, but no HTML escaping anywhere. Is this site safe from XSS?
choices: Not reliably — depending on exactly which directives are set, other injection vectors (like data exfiltration via allowed sources, or markup-only defacement) can still cause damage; CSP reduces but doesn't guarantee full protection without sanitization too
Yes — a strict CSP alone is a complete substitute for sanitizing output
Yes, as long as the site also uses HTTPS
No, but only because CSP headers are not supported by any browser
items.explanation: CSP meaningfully reduces what an injected script can do, but it isn't airtight on its own — L1/L2 are explicit that sanitization remains the primary defense, with CSP as backup, not a replacement.
items.reflection: CSP's shape — a blanket, system-enforced rule that limits what's allowed to run, independent of whatever specific bug let something sneak in — is a general defense-in-depth pattern: a firewall that limits outbound connections even if a server is compromised, or an OS permission model that limits what a malicious app can do even if it got installed. Where else have you seen a 'second independent layer' catch a failure the first layer should have prevented?

items.prompt: A team configures a CSP but allows `'unsafe-inline'` in script-src 'to avoid breaking existing code.' Does the Scenario's injected `<script>` tag still get blocked?
choices: No — allowing 'unsafe-inline' specifically permits inline scripts (like an injected `<script>` tag) to execute, defeating this particular protection
Yes — 'unsafe-inline' only affects styles, never scripts
Yes, because CSP always blocks inline scripts regardless of configuration
No, but only because 'unsafe-inline' disables CSP entirely, for every directive
items.explanation: 'unsafe-inline' does exactly what its name says — it re-permits inline script execution, which is precisely the mechanism the Scenario's injected `<script>` tag relies on.

items.prompt: Per L1, is CSP meant to be the attacker's very first obstacle, or something that matters after a different defense has already failed?
choices: Something that matters after sanitization has already failed — sanitization is the primary defense, CSP is the backstop for when it doesn't work
CSP is meant to be the very first and only defense a site needs
CSP and sanitization are applied in a fixed required order on every single request
CSP is irrelevant unless the site has no sanitization at all
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that CSP's role is as a second, independent layer in case the primary defense (sanitization) fails — it isn't meant to be the first line of defense.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what feature made the attack possible in the first place?
choices: User comments were rendered directly into the page's HTML
Users were required to log in with a weak password policy
The site used an outdated version of TLS
Comments were limited to 500 characters
items.explanation: The Scenario's root cause is rendering user comments directly as HTML, with no escaping.

items.prompt: What did the attacker submit instead of ordinary comment text?
choices: A `<script>` tag
A very long string of random characters
An image file disguised as text
A second, duplicate comment
items.explanation: The Scenario's comment contained a `<script>` tag instead of plain text.

items.prompt: Who executed the malicious script in the Scenario?
choices: Every other visitor's own browser, in their own logged-in session
Only the attacker's own browser
The site's web server, directly
No one — the script never actually ran
items.explanation: The script ran in each visitor's own browser, using their own already-logged-in session.

items.prompt: What did the script send to the attacker, per the Scenario?
choices: Each visiting user's session cookie
The site's entire source code
A list of every other comment on the page
Nothing — it only displayed a message
items.explanation: The Scenario describes the script sending each visitor's cookie to an attacker-controlled server.

items.prompt: Did the attacker directly access any other user's account credentials to pull this off?
choices: No — the attacker never touched any other user's account directly
Yes — the attacker used a leaked password list
Yes — the attacker guessed other users' passwords
There's no way to tell from the Scenario
items.explanation: The Scenario's closing question makes this explicit — no other account was touched directly.

items.prompt: Why did the victim's browser trust and run the injected script?
choices: The page treated the attacker's comment text as code instead of as plain data, so the browser ran it the same as any other script the site served
The browser has a special exception for scripts shorter than 100 characters
The victim had disabled their browser's security settings
The script was digitally signed by the attacker
items.explanation: The browser has no way to distinguish 'script the site meant to serve' from 'script smuggled in through user input' once both are rendered the same way.

items.prompt: Is this Scenario an example of 'reflected' or 'stored' XSS (covered further in L2)?
choices: Stored — the comment is saved and served to every subsequent visitor
Reflected — it required tricking one victim into clicking a link
Neither — it doesn't fit either category
Both at once
items.explanation: The comment is saved to the site's data and served to everyone who views the page — that's the stored pattern.

items.prompt: What single change would have prevented this specific Scenario's attack?
choices: Escaping the comment's text before rendering it into the page's HTML
Requiring a stronger password for commenting
Limiting comments to one per user per day
Using a faster database
items.explanation: Escaping/sanitizing the comment text before rendering is exactly the fix the Scenario calls for.

items.prompt: Suppose the Scenario's site had marked the session cookie `HttpOnly`. Would that alone have prevented the attack described?
choices: No — it would stop the script from reading `document.cookie` directly, but the script would still execute in the victim's page and could still perform actions as that user
Yes — HttpOnly completely prevents any XSS-based attack from having any effect
Yes, because HttpOnly disables JavaScript execution on the page entirely
No, but only because HttpOnly only applies to CSRF, not XSS
items.explanation: HttpOnly blocks one specific data-theft path (reading the cookie via JavaScript) — it doesn't stop the underlying script from running or from acting on the user's behalf in other ways.
items.reflection: The Scenario's real lesson is that an attacker never had to beat any authentication system directly — they got the victim's own trusted context to do the work. The same shape shows up as 'confused deputy' problems elsewhere: a service account with broad permissions being tricked into performing an action on an attacker's behalf, or a browser extension with page access being hijacked to act using the page owner's session. Where else have you seen an attacker win by riding on a victim's own legitimate trust, rather than breaking in directly?

items.prompt: If the Scenario's comment had instead been reflected back only in a URL's search results page (never saved to a database), and a victim had to click a crafted link to trigger it, would the underlying vulnerability (unescaped rendering of user input) still be XSS?
choices: Yes — it would still be XSS, specifically the reflected variant, since the root cause (unescaped user input rendered as markup) is identical; only the delivery mechanism changes
No — XSS requires permanent storage, so this would just be a browser bug
No — this would be classified as CSRF instead, since it comes from a link
Yes, but it would no longer count as a real security issue since no data is permanently stored
items.explanation: The core mechanism — unescaped user input rendered as executable markup — defines XSS regardless of whether it's delivered via stored content or a crafted link; only the classification (reflected vs. stored) changes.

items.prompt: A postmortem of the Scenario's incident concludes: 'the fix is to ban the word script from comments.' Based on everything the Scenario and L1 establish, is that an adequate fix?
choices: No — a keyword ban is a weak blocklist that's easy to bypass with different syntax (event handlers, other tags); the actual fix is escaping structural HTML characters so user text can never be parsed as markup at all
Yes — banning that one word closes off the entire attack surface
Yes, as long as the ban is case-insensitive and checks for the word in any casing
No, but only because banned words slow down comment submission too much
items.explanation: L1 and the later levels are explicit that escaping (not keyword blocking) is the real fix — a blocklist only ever covers the specific syntax someone thought to block.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does XSS need from the victim?
choices: Just viewing a page that contains the injected script
Entering their password into a fake form
Clicking a specific 'donate' button
Installing a malicious browser extension
items.explanation: L2's table is explicit: XSS just requires the victim to view a page containing the injected script.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does CSRF need from the victim?
choices: Being logged in, and interacting with (or just loading) something the attacker controls
Nothing at all — it works against logged-out visitors too
Typing their password into the attacker's own site
Installing a malicious browser extension
items.explanation: L2's table specifies CSRF needs an active logged-in session plus the victim loading or interacting with attacker-controlled content.

items.prompt: Would a CSRF token do anything to stop an injected `<script>` tag from executing?
choices: No — a CSRF token addresses forged requests, not code injection
Yes — CSRF tokens block any script execution by design
Yes, but only for scripts longer than a few lines
No, but only because CSRF tokens are deprecated
items.explanation: A CSRF token proves a request's origin — it has nothing to do with whether injected markup gets parsed and executed.

items.prompt: Would output escaping do anything to stop a forged, auto-submitting form on an attacker's page?
choices: No — escaping prevents code injection on the vulnerable site; it doesn't touch requests sent from somewhere else entirely
Yes — escaping blocks any request not originating from the site's own pages
Yes, but only for POST requests
No, but only because escaping only works on GET requests
items.explanation: Escaping is about how content is rendered on the vulnerable page — it has no bearing on a request forged and sent from a different page.

items.prompt: In the concrete CSRF example (logged into a bank, then visiting another site), what does the attacker's page actually do?
choices: Quietly submits a hidden transfer form back to the bank, relying on the browser attaching the victim's cookies automatically
Injects a script directly into the bank's own comment section
Steals the victim's password directly from their browser's memory
Sends an email to the bank asking for a password reset
items.explanation: The attacker's page submits a hidden form to the bank — it never injects anything into the bank's own site.

items.prompt: Why does the bank's server need 'another proof that the request came from the bank's own UI'?
choices: Because the browser automatically attaches the victim's cookies to the request regardless of which page actually triggered it
Because cookies expire after exactly one request
Because the bank's server can't read cookies at all
Because all requests from other sites are always rejected by default
items.explanation: Cookies travel with a request regardless of where that request originated, so a valid cookie alone doesn't prove the request came from the bank's own page.

items.prompt: Is 'exploiting a victim's logged-in session' enough on its own to tell you whether an attack is XSS or CSRF?
choices: No — both can involve a logged-in session; the distinguishing factor is the actual mechanism (injected code vs. a forged request)
Yes — any attack involving a session is automatically XSS
Yes — any attack involving a session is automatically CSRF
No, but only because sessions are irrelevant to both attacks
items.explanation: Session involvement is common to both attacks — telling them apart requires looking at the actual mechanism, not just 'a session was exploited.'

items.prompt: Does confusing XSS and CSRF as 'the same problem' lead to a working fix for both?
choices: No — each attack needs its own defense; a fix for one does nothing for the other
Yes — any single fix that blocks either attack blocks both
Yes, but only if the fix is applied twice
No, but only because no single site can ever be vulnerable to both
items.explanation: L2's failure-mode section is explicit: treating them as one problem with one fix leaves at least one of the two attacks completely unaddressed.

items.prompt: A team adds a CSRF token to every form on their site and declares 'we're now protected from XSS and CSRF.' A comment field still renders raw HTML with no escaping. Are they right?
choices: No — the CSRF token addresses CSRF only; the comment field's raw-HTML rendering is a completely separate, still-open XSS hole
Yes — a CSRF token is a complete defense against both attack types
Yes, as long as the token is also present on the comment field specifically
No, but only because CSRF tokens must be rotated more frequently to work at all
items.explanation: CSRF tokens and output escaping solve different problems — closing one leaves the other wide open; this team has only addressed half the picture.
items.reflection: Mixing up 'a defense that stops attacker code from running' with 'a defense that proves a request's origin' is a specific case of a more general trap: treating two problems that share a surface symptom (both abuse a logged-in session, here) as if they share a root cause. Where else have you seen two different failure modes get lumped into 'the same bug' because they look similar from the outside, leading to a fix that only actually addresses one of them?

items.prompt: A new engineer proposes: 'let's just block all cross-origin requests entirely — that solves CSRF, and it probably helps with XSS too, right?' Evaluate both halves of that claim.
choices: Blocking cross-origin requests is a real, relevant CSRF defense (similar in spirit to same-site cookies); but it does nothing for XSS, since an XSS payload executes as same-origin code once it's rendered into the vulnerable page itself
Both halves are correct — blocking cross-origin requests fully solves both attacks
Neither half is correct — cross-origin blocking is irrelevant to both attacks
Only the XSS half is correct; cross-origin blocking has nothing to do with CSRF
items.explanation: Cross-origin restrictions are a genuine, well-known CSRF mitigation (this is roughly what same-site cookies do) — but once an XSS payload is injected into the page, it runs as part of that page's own origin, so origin restrictions don't touch it at all.

items.prompt: A site is vulnerable to stored XSS in its bio field, and separately has no CSRF protection on its 'change email' endpoint. An attacker wants to take over an account as reliably as possible. Which attack is probably the more powerful tool here, and why?
choices: The stored XSS — a script running in the victim's own session can issue whatever authenticated requests it wants (including hitting the vulnerable change-email endpoint itself), while CSRF alone can only forge the one specific request it was built for
CSRF is strictly more powerful in every case, since it doesn't require finding an injection point
Neither is more powerful than the other — they're always functionally identical in impact
The stored XSS is irrelevant here since the vulnerable endpoint is 'change email', not 'post a comment'
items.explanation: A working XSS payload can act with the full breadth of whatever the victim's session can do — including firing off the exact forged request a CSRF attack would have needed to craft separately — making it generally the more severe primitive when both are present.

items.prompt: In reflected XSS, where does the malicious script initially live?
choices: As part of a URL or request the victim is tricked into clicking
Permanently saved in the site's own database
Only inside the attacker's own browser, never sent anywhere
In the site's server-side source code
items.explanation: Reflected XSS starts with the payload embedded in a crafted URL/request, not stored data.

items.prompt: In stored XSS, where does the malicious script live before it runs?
choices: Saved to the site's own data, such as a comment
Only in a URL the victim must click
Only in the victim's browser cache
Nowhere — it's generated fresh on each page load
items.explanation: Stored XSS persists the payload in the site's own data, unlike reflected XSS.

items.prompt: How many victims does a single reflected XSS attack typically affect per crafted link?
choices: One specific victim who clicks that link
Every visitor to the site automatically
Exactly zero, since reflected XSS never actually executes
Every visitor who has ever logged in, regardless of clicking anything
items.explanation: Reflected XSS requires one specific victim to be tricked into the crafted request — it doesn't spread to everyone automatically.

items.prompt: How many victims does a single piece of stored XSS typically affect?
choices: Every visitor who simply views the page containing it
Exactly one, the same as reflected XSS
Only the attacker who originally posted it
None, unless the victim also clicks a link
items.explanation: Stored XSS is served to everyone who views the affected page — no crafted link or click required.

items.prompt: Which generally requires more action from the victim: reflected or stored XSS?
choices: Reflected — it requires the victim to be lured into clicking a crafted link
Stored — it requires the victim to type something into a form
Neither — both require identical victim action
Stored, because it requires the victim to log in first
items.explanation: Reflected XSS depends on tricking a specific victim into a crafted click; stored XSS fires on ordinary page views.

items.prompt: Is the Scenario's comment-based attack reflected or stored XSS?
choices: Stored — the comment is saved once and served to every subsequent visitor
Reflected — the comment was part of a crafted URL
Neither — it doesn't fit either pattern
Both simultaneously
items.explanation: L2 explicitly classifies the Scenario's attack as stored XSS.

items.prompt: Does the reflected/stored distinction change what the underlying fix (escaping) looks like?
choices: No — both need the same core fix (escaping user input before rendering); what differs is persistence and how many victims are affected
Yes — reflected XSS needs escaping, but stored XSS needs a different, unrelated fix
Yes — stored XSS needs escaping, but reflected XSS can't be fixed at all
No, because neither variant can actually be fixed with escaping
items.explanation: The fix (escape before rendering) is the same for both — the distinction is about persistence and attack delivery, not about what closes the hole.

items.prompt: Why is stored XSS generally considered more severe than reflected XSS?
choices: It affects everyone who simply views the page normally, without needing to trick any specific individual
It's always technically harder for an attacker to exploit
It can only ever be fixed by taking the whole site offline
It's not actually considered more severe — severity is identical
items.explanation: Stored XSS's broader, passive reach (any normal visitor, no trick required) is exactly why it's treated as more severe.

items.prompt: A search page reflects the query string directly into an 'no results for: ...' message, unescaped. An attacker crafts a URL with a script in the query string and emails it to one target. Is this reflected or stored XSS, and does it require any permanent data on the site?
choices: Reflected — the payload travels in the URL itself and is echoed straight back; no permanent storage on the site is involved at all
Stored — any XSS involving a query parameter counts as stored by definition
Neither — query parameters can never be a vector for XSS
Both — it starts reflected but becomes stored the moment the URL is clicked once
items.explanation: Nothing is saved anywhere on the server here — the malicious script rides along in the URL and is reflected straight back into the response for that one request, which is the defining shape of reflected XSS.
items.reflection: The reflected/stored distinction is really about where state lives and who it reaches — a one-off message crafted for a specific recipient versus a persistent artifact anyone can stumble into later. That same split shows up outside security too: a one-time misconfigured email blast reaching one recipient versus a bad default saved into a shared template that silently affects everyone who uses it afterward. Where else have you seen a 'one-off, targeted' version of a mistake versus a 'persistent, affects everyone' version of the same underlying mistake?

items.prompt: A site fixes its stored XSS bug in the comment field by escaping comment text, but leaves its search-results page's unescaped query reflection completely untouched. Is the site now safe from XSS overall?
choices: No — the reflected XSS in the search page is a fully separate hole; fixing one injection point does nothing for a different, unrelated one
Yes — fixing the more severe (stored) variant automatically covers the less severe (reflected) one
Yes, because reflected XSS stopped being a real risk once the comment field was fixed
No, but only because search pages are never actually rendered as HTML
items.explanation: Each unescaped rendering point is its own independent vulnerability — fixing the comment field has no bearing on the completely separate search-results reflection bug.

items.prompt: A bug bounty report classifies a vulnerability as 'reflected XSS' but notes the payload persists across the victim's browser tab refreshes without re-clicking any link, because it's stored in the URL fragment (`#...`) which the browser keeps across reloads of that tab. Does persisting across refreshes make this actually 'stored' XSS?
choices: No — persistence in the browser's own URL bar/history for that one victim's session isn't the same as the payload being saved in the site's own backend data and served to every visitor; it's still reflected
Yes — any payload that survives a page refresh is stored XSS by definition
Yes, because the fragment is technically part of the request
No, but only because fragments are never sent to the server at all, making this not XSS at all
items.explanation: What makes XSS 'stored' is whether the payload lives in the site's own server-side data and reaches other visitors — a URL that one victim's browser happens to retain across refreshes is still a reflected, single-victim delivery mechanism, not the site persisting anything on its own.

items.prompt: Per L2, which of sanitization and CSP is described as the primary defense against XSS?
choices: Sanitization
CSP
Neither — both are described as equally optional
CSP, with sanitization as the backup
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that sanitization, done correctly, prevents the injection from happening at all — it's the primary defense.

items.prompt: Per L2, what role does CSP play relative to sanitization?
choices: A second, independent layer that helps if sanitization fails
A full replacement for sanitization
An unrelated feature with no connection to XSS defense
The only defense needed against CSRF
items.explanation: L2 frames CSP as an independent second layer, not a replacement.

items.prompt: If sanitization is implemented correctly with no bugs, does the page still need a CSP?
choices: Yes, as recommended defense-in-depth — CSP remains useful as a backstop in case a bug is introduced later
No — CSP becomes entirely pointless once sanitization is perfect
No, because CSP only matters for CSRF, not XSS
Yes, but only on pages that don't accept any user input
items.explanation: Defense-in-depth means keeping the second layer even when the first seems solid, since bugs can be introduced later.

items.prompt: Does CSP know anything about where a specific page's content comes from (e.g. which field is a 'comment')?
choices: No — it's a blanket browser-enforced rule that doesn't need application-specific knowledge
Yes — a CSP rule must be written per input field
Yes, but only for comment fields specifically
No, because CSP is applied only to CSS files, not HTML
items.explanation: CSP operates as a general rule about what's allowed to run or load, independent of any specific field's logic.

items.prompt: Can CSP alone stop a script from being injected into the page's HTML in the first place?
choices: Not reliably — CSP mainly restricts where scripts can load from and what they can do, not whether injected markup renders at all under every configuration
Yes — CSP always prevents any injected markup from rendering, full stop
Yes, but only for scripts shorter than 50 characters
No, because CSP has no effect on script execution whatsoever
items.explanation: L2 explicitly notes CSP mainly restricts sources/behavior, which isn't the same guarantee as preventing injected markup from ever rendering.

items.prompt: Would it be accurate to describe sanitization and CSP as 'two ways of doing the same thing'?
choices: No — they're independent, stacked layers that address the problem from different angles (prevent injection vs. limit damage if injection occurs)
Yes — either one alone provides identical protection
Yes, but only when both are configured with identical rules
No, because only one of the two actually relates to XSS at all
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that they're meant to work together, not as interchangeable alternatives.

items.prompt: Per L2's framing, what's the risk of relying on CSP alone without sanitizing input?
choices: An attacker can still inject script that runs in the page, since CSP mainly restricts sources/behavior rather than guaranteeing injected markup never renders
There's no risk at all — CSP alone is just as safe as sanitization alone
The only risk is slightly slower page load times
The risk only applies to sites that don't use cookies
items.explanation: L2 directly states that CSP alone, without sanitizing input, still lets an attacker inject script that runs in the page.

items.prompt: A security review finds a site has a strong CSP and no HTML escaping anywhere in its comment renderer. Management says 'the CSP covers us, we can skip the escaping work.' Evaluate that decision against L2's framing.
choices: Risky — L2 is explicit that CSP isn't a reliable substitute for sanitizing input; depending on the exact policy, injected markup can still cause real damage even under a CSP
Safe — a CSP alone is described as fully sufficient, making escaping work unnecessary
Safe, as long as the CSP is updated once a year
Risky, but only because CSP headers are deprecated in modern browsers
items.explanation: L2's whole point in pairing sanitization and CSP as independent layers is that skipping the primary layer and relying solely on the backstop is exactly the failure mode it warns against.
items.reflection: 'Having a second safety net' quietly turning into 'skipping the first one because the net exists' is a general defense-in-depth trap, not specific to web security: a team that stops writing tests because there's a staging environment that 'should catch things,' or a pilot who skips a pre-flight checklist because the autopilot 'will handle it.' Where else have you seen a backup layer get treated as a replacement for the primary one, rather than a safety net for when it fails?

items.prompt: Per L2, if a team had to pick only one of sanitization or CSP to implement (not recommended, but forced to choose), which one addresses more of the actual injection problem, and why?
choices: Sanitization — it prevents the injection from happening at all, whereas CSP only limits what an injected script can do once it's already present
CSP — it's described as the more fundamental of the two defenses
Neither — L2 treats them as fully interchangeable, with no meaningful difference in coverage
Sanitization, but only because CSP requires a paid license to use
items.explanation: L2 frames sanitization as the primary defense that prevents injection outright — CSP is explicitly the secondary, damage-limiting layer, not the more foundational one.

items.prompt: A junior engineer argues: 'if we have a good CSP, the specific escaping function we use for comments doesn't really matter much.' Using L2's reasoning, what's the flaw in this argument?
choices: CSP doesn't reliably prevent injected markup from rendering at all under every configuration — if the escaping function itself is wrong or incomplete, the injection can still happen, and CSP only limits (doesn't guarantee zero) damage from there
There's no flaw — CSP makes the specific escaping implementation irrelevant
The flaw is only that CSP headers need to be set per-page, not site-wide
The flaw is that escaping functions are always perfect by construction, so this concern never arises in practice
items.explanation: L2's stacked-layers model only works if each layer actually does its job — a broken or incomplete escaping function is still a real injection, and CSP was never designed to be a complete guarantee against all consequences of that.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what goes wrong when treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem with one shared fix?
choices: Sanitizing displayed content does nothing to prevent a forged authenticated request, and a CSRF token does nothing to stop an injected script from executing
Nothing goes wrong — a shared fix is described as fully adequate for both
The issue only matters for sites with no login system at all
The issue is purely a naming/terminology problem, not a security one
items.explanation: L2 explicitly states each fix addresses a different mechanism — one doesn't substitute for the other.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of assuming only permanently stored input needs sanitizing?
choices: Reflected XSS shows that even data that's never saved can still be dangerous if it's echoed back into a page unescaped
There's no risk — only stored input is ever actually dangerous
The risk only applies to sites using a specific database technology
This assumption is actually the recommended approach per L2
items.explanation: L2 uses reflected XSS as the direct counterexample to this assumption.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with treating CSP as a substitute for sanitizing input?
choices: CSP reduces the damage an injected script can do; it doesn't reliably prevent the injection from happening in the first place
Nothing is wrong — CSP is described as a complete substitute for sanitization
This is only a problem for sites that don't use HTTPS
CSP has no actual relationship to injected scripts at all
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that CSP limits damage rather than reliably preventing the injection itself.

items.prompt: Which of these three failure modes involves confusing two attacks that need genuinely different fixes?
choices: Treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem with one shared fix
Assuming only stored input needs sanitizing
Treating CSP as a substitute for sanitizing input
None of them involve confusing two different attacks
items.explanation: The XSS/CSRF conflation is specifically about mixing up two different attacks and their defenses.

items.prompt: Which failure mode is most directly illustrated by a crafted-link attack that never gets permanently saved anywhere?
choices: Assuming only stored input needs sanitizing
Treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem
Treating CSP as a substitute for sanitization
None of the above
items.explanation: A crafted link that's never stored but still dangerous is exactly the reflected-XSS counterexample to the 'only stored input matters' assumption.

items.prompt: A team configures a strict CSP and declares their escaping work 'no longer necessary.' Which failure mode from L2 does this match?
choices: Treating CSP as a substitute for sanitizing input
Treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem
Assuming only stored input needs sanitizing
None of these — this is a reasonable, safe call
items.explanation: Dropping sanitization because a CSP exists is precisely the third failure mode L2 names.

items.prompt: A team uses a CSRF token to 'fix' a comment field that renders raw HTML. Which failure mode does this match?
choices: Treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem with one shared fix
Treating CSP as a substitute for sanitizing input
Assuming only stored input needs sanitizing
None of these — a CSRF token is a valid fix for unescaped HTML
items.explanation: Applying a CSRF-specific fix to an XSS-shaped problem is the first failure mode — the two need genuinely different defenses.

items.prompt: Do these three failure modes, taken together, point to one single underlying theme?
choices: Yes — assuming a defense's scope is broader than it actually is, instead of matching each specific mechanism to its own specific fix
No — they're three completely unrelated mistakes with nothing in common
Yes, but only because all three happen to involve cookies
No, because only one of the three is a genuine mistake
items.explanation: Each failure mode is a version of over-generalizing one defense's coverage — assuming it covers more of the problem than it actually does.

items.prompt: A postmortem lists three root causes for a breach: (1) a CSRF token was used to 'fix' a raw-HTML comment field, (2) only the comment field was escaped, not the search page's reflected query, and (3) a CSP was added and escaping was then removed entirely. Map each to one of L2's three named failure modes.
choices: (1) treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem; (2) assuming only stored input needs sanitizing; (3) treating CSP as a substitute for sanitization
All three map to the same single failure mode: insufficient testing
(1) and (2) are the same failure mode; (3) is unrelated to anything in L2
None of these map cleanly to L2's failure modes — they're all genuinely new mistakes
items.explanation: Each of the three postmortem causes is a near-direct match to one of L2's three explicitly named failure modes — a CSRF-shaped fix for an XSS-shaped bug, under-scoping sanitization to only stored fields, and conflating CSP with a replacement for escaping.
items.reflection: All three failure modes share a shape: a real defense gets applied confidently, but outside the specific scope where it actually works. That's a pattern well beyond security — a caching strategy that assumes 'the data rarely changes' applied to a field that actually changes constantly, or a code review checklist built for one kind of bug applied uncritically to a different kind of bug it was never designed to catch. Where else have you seen a correct tool or fix get over-applied beyond the specific problem it was actually built to solve?

items.prompt: A site has escaped every comment field and every reflected query parameter (closing both stored and reflected XSS), has a correct CSRF token on every state-changing form, and has also kept a strict CSP as a backstop. Per L2, is any of the three named failure modes still present?
choices: No — this setup correctly matches each attack to its own defense and keeps CSP as a genuine backstop rather than a replacement for anything
Yes — using both a CSRF token and CSP at the same time is itself the first failure mode
Yes — escaping both stored and reflected input is redundant and matches the second failure mode
Yes — keeping CSP alongside full escaping always matches the third failure mode
items.explanation: This setup is exactly the intended end state L2 describes: distinct, correctly-scoped fixes for XSS (escaping, comprehensive) and CSRF (tokens), with CSP kept as an independent backstop rather than a substitute for anything — none of the three failure modes apply.

items.prompt: A new hire asks: 'if I only have time to fix one of these three failure modes before a security audit, which one most directly risks a full account takeover, rather than just one feature breaking?' Reason through which of the three poses the broadest risk, based on L2's content.
choices: Treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem is the broadest risk, since leaving either XSS or CSRF effectively unaddressed can let an attacker act with a victim's full session privileges, not just affect one narrow feature
Assuming only stored input needs sanitizing is clearly the least risky of the three and can be skipped entirely
All three are exactly equally risky in every conceivable scenario, with no meaningful way to prioritize
Treating CSP as a substitute for sanitization is irrelevant to account takeover risk
items.explanation: Confusing XSS and CSRF defenses risks leaving either attack's actual mechanism (code execution or forged authenticated requests) completely unaddressed — either one, left open, can translate into broad account-level compromise, not just a narrow feature bug.

items.prompt: What does `renderCommentVulnerable` do with `comment.text`?
choices: Inserts it directly into the HTML string with no transformation at all
Encrypts it before inserting it into the page
Strips out any character that isn't a letter or number
Rejects any comment longer than 200 characters
items.explanation: The vulnerable renderer does a direct, unmodified string insertion — that's the entire bug.

items.prompt: When a `<script>` tag sits inside `comment.text` and gets inserted this way, what does it become in the rendered page?
choices: A real, executable `<script>` tag, part of the actual markup
Plain visible text reading '<script>'
An HTML comment that the browser ignores
A broken tag that the browser silently discards
items.explanation: Because there's no escaping, the characters are parsed as real markup, producing a genuine executable script tag.

items.prompt: Does the browser know or care that the `<script>` tag originally came from user input rather than from the site's own code?
choices: No — it just runs it, the same way it would run any script the site itself served
Yes — browsers refuse to execute any script tag that originated from a comment field
Yes, but only if the script is longer than 100 characters
No, but only because this specific browser has a bug
items.explanation: The browser has no mechanism to distinguish 'legitimate site script' from 'script smuggled in through user input' once both are rendered the same way.

items.prompt: What does `document.cookie` give the injected script access to, in the Scenario's exploit?
choices: The victim's own session cookie for that site
The attacker's own session cookie
A list of every cookie from every website the victim has ever visited
Nothing — document.cookie never returns anything useful
items.explanation: document.cookie exposes the current page's own cookies — here, the victim's session cookie for the vulnerable site.

items.prompt: Does marking the session cookie `HttpOnly` make the underlying XSS vulnerability itself go away?
choices: No — it blocks one specific data-theft path (reading via document.cookie), but the injected script is still running inside the victim's page
Yes — HttpOnly fully closes the vulnerability
Yes, because HttpOnly disables script execution for the whole page
No, but only because HttpOnly only works on HTTPS sites
items.explanation: HttpOnly only blocks one consequence (cookie theft via JS) — the script itself is still executing with the victim's privileges.

items.prompt: According to L3, is the vulnerable HTML in this example being inserted via `innerHTML`, or as the page's initial HTML?
choices: As the page's initial HTML — which is why the injected `<script>` tag actually runs
Via `innerHTML`, which is why it runs
Neither — the example never specifies how the HTML reaches the page
It doesn't matter at all for whether the script executes
items.explanation: L3 specifically notes this is served as the initial page HTML, not inserted later via innerHTML, which is part of why the script tag executes.

items.prompt: Per L3, if the malicious markup were inserted later via `innerHTML` instead of being part of the initial page load, would a `<script>` tag inside it execute?
choices: No — browsers deliberately don't execute `<script>` tags inserted via innerHTML
Yes — innerHTML always executes any script tag it's given
Yes, but only in older browsers
No, but only because innerHTML is disabled by default
items.explanation: L3 explicitly calls out that browsers deliberately skip executing script tags inserted via innerHTML — though other vectors like event-handler attributes can still be dangerous that way.

items.prompt: Does the innerHTML detail mean user input inserted that way is always safe?
choices: No — other injected markup, like event-handler attributes, can still be dangerous even via innerHTML
Yes — innerHTML insertion is completely immune to any XSS risk
Yes, but only for text shorter than 50 characters
No, but only because innerHTML is deprecated
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that this is not a safety rule — other injection vectors remain dangerous through innerHTML.

items.prompt: A developer argues: 'the real bug here is that we used a template literal — if we'd built the HTML with string concatenation instead, this wouldn't happen.' Is that correct?
choices: No — the vulnerability is inserting unescaped user input into any string that becomes real HTML markup; the specific string-building syntax (template literal vs. concatenation) makes no difference to the outcome
Yes — template literals are uniquely responsible for enabling XSS, and concatenation is immune
Yes, but only because template literals run inside Node.js differently from the browser
No, but only because concatenation is actually slower, not safer
items.explanation: The mechanism is about what's inserted and how it's escaped, not which JavaScript syntax is used to build the string — switching to concatenation with the same unescaped value produces an identical vulnerability.
items.reflection: The core insight here — a string only becomes 'code' because of the parser that reads it next, never because of anything inherent in the characters — generalizes past HTML: the same bytes are inert in a log file but dangerous as a shell command argument, or inert as JSON but dangerous as a template string that gets eval'd. Where else have you seen the exact same data be perfectly safe in one context and dangerous the moment it lands in a different one?

items.prompt: Suppose `renderCommentVulnerable`'s output is sent to the browser as a JSON API response (`{"html": "<div>...<script>..."}`), not rendered directly as a page. Is the XSS risk eliminated just by that change?
choices: Not necessarily — the risk depends on what the client does with that HTML string next; if the client ever inserts it into the DOM as markup (e.g. via innerHTML or a templating function that doesn't escape), the same vulnerability reappears on the client side
Yes — JSON responses can never contain anything dangerous, by definition
Yes, because JSON automatically escapes every string it contains
No, but only because JSON responses are always rejected by modern browsers
items.explanation: Wrapping the same unescaped HTML in a JSON envelope doesn't change what happens once a client takes that string and renders it as markup — the vulnerability just moves to wherever the unescaped insertion actually happens.

items.prompt: A monitoring dashboard renders third-party log lines directly into the page to make them easy to read, with no escaping, reasoning 'logs aren't user input, so this is safe.' Is that reasoning sound, given what made the Scenario's renderer vulnerable?
choices: No — the vulnerable mechanism is unescaped text being rendered as markup, regardless of whether the source is literally called 'user input'; if any part of a log line is attacker-influenced (e.g. a username, request path, or header an attacker controls), it's just as dangerous
Yes — logs are generated by the server, so by definition they can never contain attacker-controlled content
Yes, as long as the logs are stored in a database rather than a flat file
No, but only because dashboards never use HTML rendering at all
items.explanation: The mechanism doesn't care what the data is 'called' — if any attacker-reachable value (a header, a path, a username that ends up logged) is rendered unescaped, the exact same renderer-level bug applies, log line or not.

items.prompt: Complete `escapeAmp` so it replaces every `&` with `&`.
items.explanation: A global regex replace on `&` is the first step — it has to run before any other replacement, since every other entity itself contains an `&`.

items.prompt: Complete `escapeLt` so it replaces every `<` with `<`.
items.explanation: `<` is the character that opens an HTML tag — replacing it with its entity is what stops a string from being parsed as a tag.

items.prompt: Complete `escapeGt` so it replaces every `>` with `>`.
items.explanation: `>` closes a tag — escaping it alongside `<` is what prevents a full `<script>...</script>` pair from being parsed as real markup.

items.prompt: Complete `escapeQuote` so it replaces every `"` with `"`.
items.explanation: Double quotes matter specifically in attribute contexts (`title="..."`) — leaving them unescaped lets an attacker break out of an attribute value.

items.prompt: Complete `escapeSingleQuote` so it replaces every `'` with `'`.
items.explanation: Single quotes need the same treatment as double quotes, since attributes can be delimited by either one.

items.prompt: Complete `escapeHtmlOrdered` so it escapes `&` before any of the other four characters (`<`, `>`, `"`, `'`).
items.explanation: Replacing `&` first means any `&` introduced by the later replacements (like the `&` in `<`) never gets escaped a second time — order matters here.

items.prompt:
Complete `renderEscaped(text)` so it returns `
` + the escaped text + `
`, using a provided `escapeHtml` helper.

tests.description: wraps escaped text in the comment div

items.explanation: This mirrors the fix from the unit: the same template-literal shape as the vulnerable renderer, but the value passed in is escaped first.

items.prompt: Complete `isFullyEscaped(str)` so it returns `true` only if the string contains no literal `<` or `>` characters.

tests.description: passes a string with only entities

items.explanation: A simple way to sanity-check escaping worked: the output should contain no raw structural characters at all, only their entity equivalents.

items.prompt: Write `escapeHtml(str)` so it replaces all five structural HTML characters (&, <, >, ", ') with their literal text equivalents, escaping & first.

tests.description: a script tag is fully escaped, with no literal < remaining
the escaped output preserves the original text as literal characters
ampersands and quotes are also escaped correctly

items.explanation: Replacing the characters that give HTML its structural meaning with their literal text equivalents means a browser renders them as visible text instead of interpreting them as markup — the content is preserved exactly, but it can never be parsed as a tag.
items.reflection: Writing the escaping function by hand makes the mapping concrete, but the deeper idea — neutralize exactly the characters that are structurally meaningful in the destination format, before the data crosses into it — applies well beyond HTML: escaping a shell argument (quotes and `$`), parameterizing a SQL query instead of concatenating a string, or escaping regex metacharacters before using user input as a literal pattern. Where else have you seen 'figure out which characters are structurally special in the target format, then neutralize exactly those' show up as the real fix?

items.prompt: Write `escapeHtml(str)` so it correctly handles an attacker's attribute-breakout attempt: `' onmouseover='alert(1)` should come out with both single quotes escaped and no raw quote character remaining.

tests.description: single-quoted attribute breakout is escaped, no raw ' remains
a plain script tag is still escaped correctly too

items.explanation: An attribute-breakout payload doesn't need any `<` or `>` at all — it just needs the same quote character the attribute is delimited by; escaping both quote characters (not only angle brackets) closes this specific vector.

items.prompt: Write `escapeHtml(str)` and confirm it does NOT double-escape an `&` that was introduced by one of its own replacements (e.g. escaping `<` should not then re-escape the `&` inside the resulting `<`).

tests.description: escaping < once does not double-escape the resulting &
a pre-existing literal & is correctly escaped exactly once
mixed input escapes correctly without double-escaping

items.explanation: If `&` weren't replaced first, escaping `<` into `<` would introduce a fresh `&` that a later `&` replacement pass would then re-escape into `&lt;` — corrupting the output; ordering the `&` replacement first avoids this entirely.

items.prompt: What does the `script-src` CSP directive control?
choices: Where executable scripts are allowed to load from
Which fonts the page is allowed to display
How long a session cookie is allowed to live
Which countries are allowed to access the page
items.explanation: script-src specifically governs allowed sources for scripts.

items.prompt: What does `default-src` do when a more specific directive (like `script-src`) isn't set?
choices: It acts as the fallback source list for that unset directive
It overrides every other directive, even ones that are set
It disables CSP entirely
It only applies to image resources
items.explanation: default-src is the fallback used when a more specific directive is absent.

items.prompt: What does `'self'` mean inside a CSP source list?
choices: Resources from the site's own origin are allowed
Any resource from anywhere is allowed
Only resources served over HTTP (not HTTPS) are allowed
No resources at all are allowed
items.explanation: 'self' permits the page's own origin as a valid source.

items.prompt: If `script-src` is set to `'self' https://cdn.example.com` with no `'unsafe-inline'`, would an inline `<script>alert(1)</script>` injected directly into the page's HTML be allowed to run?
choices: No — it has no external source at all, and 'unsafe-inline' isn't present
Yes — 'self' always permits inline scripts too
Yes, as long as the script is shorter than 200 characters
No, but only because alert() is specifically blocked by CSP
items.explanation: Without 'unsafe-inline', an inline script with no external source is blocked under a script-src like this.

items.prompt: What does adding `'unsafe-inline'` to `script-src` do?
choices: Re-permits inline scripts and inline event handlers to execute
Blocks all scripts regardless of source
Only allows scripts from the exact same page URL
Disables CSP checking for images only
items.explanation: 'unsafe-inline' specifically re-enables inline script execution, which a stricter policy would otherwise block.

items.prompt: Who is actually responsible for enforcing a site's CSP once the header is sent?
choices: The visitor's browser
The site's own backend server, continuously
A third-party CDN
The site's database
items.explanation: CSP enforcement happens client-side, in the browser, based on the header the server sent.

items.prompt: Does an inline event-handler attribute like `onerror='...'` count as 'inline script' from CSP's point of view?
choices: Yes — it's script content embedded directly in the page's HTML, the same as an inline `<script>` block
No — only `<script>` tags are covered by script-src, never event handlers
No, because event handlers are considered CSS, not JavaScript
Yes, but only in Internet Explorer
items.explanation: CSP treats inline event-handler attributes as inline script, just like a `<script>` block — both are blocked by the same script-src rule.

items.prompt: Would a CSP need to know anything about a site's specific comment-rendering code to block an injected inline script there?
choices: No — it's a blanket rule based on source/type, not specific application logic
Yes — a separate script-src rule must be written for every input field
Yes, but only for comment fields specifically
No, because CSP only ever applies to login forms
items.explanation: CSP operates generically on what's allowed to execute and from where — it doesn't need to know which specific feature produced the markup.

items.prompt: A policy sets `script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com 'unsafe-inline'`. Would this policy have blocked the Scenario's injected `<script>` tag?
choices: No — 'unsafe-inline' specifically re-permits inline scripts, which is exactly what the Scenario's injected tag is
Yes — 'self' and the CDN source override 'unsafe-inline' and block it anyway
Yes, because injected script is always blocked regardless of policy wording
No, but only because the policy is also missing a default-src directive
items.explanation: Including 'unsafe-inline' defeats this specific protection — the Scenario's attack relies on exactly the inline-script execution that 'unsafe-inline' re-enables.
items.reflection: A permission list that quietly includes a broad escape hatch (here, 'unsafe-inline') undermining the whole point of the list is a general pattern in access control: a firewall rule set that's mostly strict except for one '0.0.0.0/0' entry someone added to 'get something working,' or a least-privilege IAM policy with one wildcard permission left over from debugging. Where else have you seen a single broad exception quietly undo an otherwise well-designed restriction?

items.prompt: A team wants to keep using a handful of small inline `<script>` snippets they've written themselves (not user-controlled), without allowing an attacker's injected inline script to run. Is 'just allow unsafe-inline for our own snippets, block everyone else's' a coherent option under CSP?
choices: Not really — CSP's script-src can't distinguish 'our own inline script' from 'attacker-injected inline script' by origin, since both are inline; the real mechanisms for this are a per-script cryptographic hash/nonce allow-list, or moving the snippets to an external file under an allowed source
Yes — CSP automatically recognizes which inline scripts were written by the site's own developers
Yes, as long as the inline scripts are placed before the injected ones in the HTML
No, because CSP can never allow any inline script under any circumstances, even with nonces or hashes
items.explanation: script-src's inline-vs-not distinction doesn't know 'who wrote it' — permitting specific inline scripts safely requires nonces or hashes (tying the permission to the exact approved script content), not a blanket 'unsafe-inline' that opens the door to everything inline, injected or not.

items.prompt: A site's CSP only sets `img-src 'self'` and leaves `script-src` completely unset, with no `default-src` either. Per how directives fall back to default-src, is this site's script execution restricted at all by this policy?
choices: No — with no script-src and no default-src set, script execution isn't restricted by this policy at all; img-src only governs image sources
Yes — img-src automatically restricts scripts too, since it's the first directive listed
Yes, because any CSP header at all blocks every inline script by default
No, but only because img-src overrides script-src whenever both would otherwise apply
items.explanation: Each directive only governs its own resource category — setting img-src says nothing about scripts, and without a default-src fallback either, script execution here is effectively unrestricted by this policy.

items.prompt: Per L3's closing section, does the core lesson ('user input rendered into a page must be treated as inert data, never executable markup') apply only to comment sections?
choices: No — it generalizes to any place user content gets displayed: search results, profiles, chat messages, file names
Yes — it applies exclusively to comment fields
Yes, but only to fields explicitly labeled 'comment'
No, but only because comment fields are being phased out
items.explanation: L3 explicitly generalizes the lesson beyond comments to any displayed user content.

items.prompt: Does the exact `escapeHtml` function used in this unit work correctly for every possible place user data might be inserted into a page?
choices: No — a different context (an HTML attribute, a script block, a URL) needs its own context-specific escaping approach
Yes — the same function is universally correct for every HTML context
Yes, as long as the input is always under 500 characters
No, but only because the function has a bug unrelated to context
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that this escapeHtml handles one specific context (element text content); other contexts need different handling.
