items.prompt: Which HTML context does this unit's `escapeHtml` specifically handle?
choices: Inserting text into an HTML element's body/text content
Inserting text into a `<script>` block
Inserting text into a URL
Inserting text into a CSS value
items.explanation: L3 names this specifically as the context escapeHtml was built for — not attribute values, script blocks, or URLs.

items.prompt: If a comment's author name were inserted into an HTML attribute (e.g. `<div title="${comment.author}">`), would the same escapeHtml necessarily be fully sufficient?
choices: Not necessarily — attribute context has its own structural characters (the quote delimiting the attribute) that need the same care, and L3 poses this exact question as something to work through, not something already answered for you
Yes — escapeHtml is always sufficient in every HTML context without exception
No, because attributes can never contain any user-supplied content at all
Yes, but only if the attribute name is 'title' specifically
items.explanation: L3 raises this exact scenario as an open question for the reader to reason through — attribute context introduces its own structural characters that need matching care.

items.prompt: What's the relationship between 'this worked example' and 'the whole territory' of injection contexts, per L3?
choices: The worked example is a case, not the whole territory — L3 says this explicitly
The worked example covers every possible injection context completely
There's no meaningful relationship — each context is entirely unrelated to the others
The worked example is only relevant to attribute contexts, not element text
items.explanation: L3 explicitly frames its one worked example as a case study, not exhaustive coverage of every injection context.

items.prompt: Does the core lesson change depending on which specific rendering context is involved (element text vs. attribute vs. script block)?
choices: No — the core lesson (never treat user input as executable markup) stays the same; what changes is which specific characters matter structurally in that context
Yes — each context requires an entirely different core lesson with no shared principle
Yes, but only for attribute contexts specifically
No, and the specific escaping characters never change by context either
items.explanation: The underlying principle is constant; only the context-specific mechanics (which characters are structurally dangerous) differ.

items.prompt: A developer uses this unit's element-text `escapeHtml` to sanitize a value inserted into a URL query string being built server-side (e.g. `href="/search?q=${escapeHtml(userInput)}"`). Is this necessarily safe?
choices: Not necessarily — a URL context has its own structurally dangerous characters (like `&`, which separates query parameters, or characters needing percent-encoding) that HTML-text escaping doesn't address; an attacker could still manipulate the URL's structure even though no HTML tag forms
Yes — escapeHtml is a universal sanitizer that covers every context a value could ever be inserted into
Yes, because any value inside an href attribute is automatically safe regardless of escaping
No, but only because href attributes are deprecated in modern HTML
items.explanation: HTML-text escaping and URL encoding solve different structural problems — a value can be perfectly safe as HTML text while still corrupting the URL's own structure (extra query parameters, a scheme change) if it isn't also properly URL-encoded for that context.
items.reflection: Matching the fix to the exact context the data lands in — not just 'sanitize it somewhere' — is a recurring discipline: the same user-supplied string might need HTML-escaping before display, parameterization before a SQL query, and shell-escaping before a subprocess call, all for the same underlying value used three different ways downstream. Where else have you seen a single piece of untrusted data need a different, context-specific treatment depending on where it ends up being used?

items.prompt: Suppose the Scenario's comment author's display name, instead of the news being 'good' or routine, carried a legitimately adversarial, highly motivated attacker testing every input field on the site systematically. If the same renderer escapes the comment body correctly but never escapes the author name field, what's the actual exposure, reasoned from L3's generalization section rather than anything specific to the comment body?
choices: The exposure is identical in kind to the original Scenario — any unescaped field rendered as markup is a full XSS vector, regardless of which specific field it is or how motivated the attacker happens to be
There's no exposure, since the author name field is shorter than the comment body and can't carry a full payload
The exposure is lower because display names are usually validated to be real human names
There's no exposure because only the single field explicitly named 'comment' in the Scenario can ever be dangerous
items.explanation: L3's generalization is explicit that the lesson applies to any displayed user content, not the one field the Scenario happened to use as its illustration — an unescaped author-name field is exactly as exploitable as the comment body was.

items.prompt: A file-upload feature inserts the uploaded file's name into the page (e.g. "You uploaded: FILENAME") using this unit's element-text escapeHtml, and separately inserts that same filename into a `<script>` block as a JSON-like value for a client-side analytics call. Does escaping it once for display cover the second use too?
choices: No — a `<script>` block has entirely different structural rules (quotes, backslashes, and sequences like `</script>` need JS-string-safe escaping, not HTML-entity escaping); the same raw filename needs to be escaped separately, appropriately, for each context it lands in
Yes — once a value is HTML-escaped, it's automatically safe in every other context it's ever inserted into
Yes, because file names can never contain any character that would matter in a script context
No, but only because analytics scripts are exempt from needing any escaping at all
items.explanation: Each insertion point is its own context with its own structurally dangerous characters — HTML-text escaping doesn't make a value safe inside a `<script>` block, where quotes, backslashes, and the literal sequence `</script>` are the structurally meaningful characters instead.
